growth_story.headline: After a flat decade and a debt crisis, Portugal's income per person reached a new high in 2025, though its growth has slowed each year since 2022.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990 Portugal's income per person has grown 1.4 percent a year, with no lasting shift in pace, but that single era hides sharp swings. Growth ran at 3.1 to 4.3 percent a year from 1995 to 1999, then stalled in the early 2000s, and the IMF notes that labor productivity has lagged European peers for two decades. Over 2006 to 2015 income per person did not grow at all, averaging 0.0 percent a year: it fell 3.2 percent in 2009 and, during the sovereign debt crisis, 3.7 percent in 2012, while investment dropped from 28.0 percent of GDP in 2000 to 14.8 percent in 2013. The last decade was better, at 1.8 percent a year, with growth of 3.6 percent in 2017, a fall of 8.3 percent in the 2020 pandemic and rebounds of 4.9 and 6.2 percent in 2021 and 2022. The IMF links the recent run to strong consumption, net exports, investment backed by EU funds, tourism and net migration, and income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025, even as its growth slowed to 0.8 percent that year.

threads.title: Debt crisis and deep recessions
threads.text: Portugal went through two deep recessions in a decade: the sovereign debt crisis of 2011 to 2013 and the 2020 pandemic. In the data, income per person fell in 2011, 2012 and 2013 and dropped 8.3 percent in 2020. Portugal's executive director at the IMF credits the later recovery partly to the adjustments made after the debt crisis.

citations.quote: two deep recessions that Portugal experienced in the past decade (with a cumulative real GDP contraction of 6.6 percent during 2011–13

threads.title: Productivity that lags peers
threads.text: The IMF finds that Portugal has trailed its European peers in output per worker for two decades, partly because of many small firms and resources going to less productive firms, but mostly because of weak productivity inside firms. It expects an aging population, low investment and slow productivity growth to hold growth below 2 percent over the medium term.

citations.title: IMF Country Report No. 24/308 Portugal: 2024 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Portugal
citations.quote: Portugal has lagged its European peers in labor productivity over the last two decades, despite recent progress in upskilling the labor force

citations.title: IMF Country Report No. 24/308 Portugal: 2024 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Portugal
citations.quote: This productivity gap is partially explained by resource misallocation and the predominance of small firms, while weak within- firm productivity remains a dominant factor.

citations.title: Portugal: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2026 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: Over the medium term, population aging, relatively low investment levels, and low productivity growth are expected to keep growth below 2 percent.

threads.title: Migration offsets an aging population
threads.text: Portugal's own working-age population is shrinking, but large net migration has more than made up for it, raising hours worked. The IMF still expects the working-age population to fall faster than in the euro area over time.

citations.title: IMF Country Report No. 24/308 Portugal: 2024 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Portugal
citations.quote: Large positive net migration has more than mitigated a shrinking domestic working-age population, resulting in a positive working-age population growth in 2023.

citations.title: IMF Country Report No. 24/308 Portugal: 2024 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Portugal
citations.quote: Increasing labor force participation and net positive migration led to higher hours worked while unemployment remains at historically low levels.

citations.title: IMF Country Report No. 24/308 Portugal: 2024 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Portugal

threads.title: EU funds and tourism
threads.text: The IMF ties the post-pandemic run to strong consumption, net exports and investment paid for by EU funds, and expects strong tourism to keep the current account in surplus. Investment in the data has climbed back from 14.8 percent of GDP in 2013 to 20.7 percent in 2025. The IMF expects growth to ease as the EU recovery funds end.

citations.title: IMF Country Report No. 24/308 Portugal: 2024 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Portugal
citations.quote: driven by strong private consumption, net exports, and investment supported by EU funds.

threads.title: Public debt falls fast
threads.text: Public debt has fallen sharply since 2020, alongside three budget surpluses in a row. The IMF still describes the debt as high.

since_last_year.text: The IMF's 2026 review found that GDP grew faster than the euro area average in 2025. It expects growth to ease in 2027 as EU recovery funds end. In the data, growth in income per person slowed to 0.8 percent in 2025, from 1.1 percent in 2024.

growth_story.tension: The IMF reports that GDP grew faster than the euro area average in 2025. Yet income per person grew only 0.8 percent in 2025, down from 6.2 percent in 2022, and has slowed every year since. The IMF's 2024 report notes that net migration was enlarging the working-age population, and when the population grows, total output can rise faster than income per person.
